title: Build your own agent
description: How the parts of the course (the task, the tools, the way it answers, how much it acts alone, the model) come together into your own agent: a chat with the Builder, a review screen, and publishing.

steps.question: You already know about context, memory, tools, skills and hooks one by one. What if you put them together into YOUR own agent?
steps.answer: That is what the builder is for. It is not a form with a dozen fields. It is a conversation: you say what you need, a built-in helper asks questions with tick boxes, and at the end you review and publish it yourself. Almost every question is something you have already learned.

steps.text: An agent is not magic. It is a set of understandable parts: what it does (its role and instructions), what it uses (tools), how it answers (length, format, tone), when it acts on its own (reminders, background checks) and which model it runs on. The Builder asks about these parts one by one.

steps.imagePrompt: A construction kit laid out on a table: parts of a small friendly robot ready to be assembled, including a head with a theatre mask, a rolled instruction scroll, a tool belt, a looping gear and a small shield.
steps.caption: An agent is put together from understandable parts

steps.definition: A built-in helper called the Builder (it runs on Muse Spark by default). It asks one question at a time with three or four tick boxes and writes a draft of your agent, with no code. It cannot publish the agent. You do that yourself, on the review screen.
steps.example: You write: “I want an agent that tracks my spending.” The Builder asks about tools, and you tick “Memory” and “Reminders.” That is how the agent gets its hands.

steps.instruction: Put the steps in the order the Builder goes through them:
items: How to answer: length, format, tone
What the agent should do, in your own words
Review: the draft, a dry run, publishing
Which model: Spark, Wonder or the app default
When to act on its own: reminders and background checks, or never
steps.explain: First you say what the agent should do. Then the Builder asks about tools, the way it answers, how much it acts alone, and the model. At the end you review the draft, try it out, and publish it yourself.

steps.text: You start with free text. Tap “Create agent” on the Agents tab, and a chat with the Builder opens. It says hello and asks just one thing: what should the agent do? You answer in plain words. From your answer it fills in the name, the description and the instructions, which are the system prompt, or the agent's character. Good instructions start with a role or a task, then set the format, the length and the tone.

After that comes one question at a time, each with three or four tick boxes. Which tools the agent may use: these are its hands. How it should answer. When it should act on its own: reminders and background checks, or never. Which model: Muse Wonder for long, multi-step work, Muse Spark for faster and cheaper work, or the app default. The Builder ticks the likely options in advance, so you only adjust them. Each agent has its own memory: it cannot see other agents' memories, and it only reads your shared profile if you turn that on. Modes and rules (hooks) are not set in the chat. You can see them on the review screen.

steps.caption: Add parts and run a test at any time: watch how the agent's answer changes

steps.situation: The Builder has written a draft and shown a “Review your agent” card. You want to publish it right away and start using it.
steps.q: What is the sensible first thing to do on the review screen?
options: Run a dry run on a real task and adjust the settings
Tap Publish at once: the Builder already checked everything
Ask the Builder in the chat to publish the agent for you
steps.explain: A dry run is a test drive: you run the draft on a real task and fix things while the agent is still unpublished. The Builder cannot publish for you. It is always your tap.

steps.text: The card opens the review screen. It shows every setting on one page: the name, the instructions, the tools as tick boxes, the modes, the model and the rules. You can change anything right there. The rules (hooks) are listed, and the “Edit rules” button takes you to their editor. The “Try it” dry run and the Publish button are on this page too. If you prefer the old step-by-step form, tap “Edit step by step.” After you publish, the agent appears in “My agents” and you can use it from a chat. If you gave it a proactive tool, it can remind you and wake up on a schedule by itself. You have built a small app for your own task without writing a line of code.

Practice. Open the Agents tab and tap “Create agent.” Describe the job in your own words, for example: “Keep track of my spending and remind me in the evening to log expenses.” Answer the questions with ticks: the tools “Memory” and “Reminders,” a shorter answer, and reminders for acting on its own. When the “Review your agent” card appears, open it. In the “Modes” section allow “Plan” and “Goal,” which you will need in the next lessons. Then give the agent a task in “Try it.” Tap Publish only when you are happy with the answer. Don't be afraid to make a mistake: until you publish, it is only a draft.

In short. Building an agent means deciding five things: what it does, what it uses, how it answers, when it acts on its own, and which model it runs on. “Create agent” opens a chat with the Builder, which asks one question at a time with tick boxes and writes a draft, but cannot publish. The review screen shows every setting and the rules (“Edit rules”), and has the “Try it” dry run. You publish it yourself, and the agent then lives in “My agents.” Each agent has its own memory compartment.

questions.q: What does the Agent Builder do?
options: Asks questions with tick boxes and writes a draft of your agent
Publishes the finished agent to your set by itself
Writes the agent's code in Kotlin and builds an app
questions.explain: The Builder holds a conversation: one question at a time, with tick-box options, and a draft at the end. You don't need to write code, and you publish it yourself.

questions.q: Why is there a review screen before publishing?
options: To see every setting and try the draft out in action
To save the agent's settings on a remote server
To check that your Meta Model API key still works
questions.explain: The review screen is a test drive for the draft: you see every setting, run a dry run, and catch mistakes before the agent is published.

questions.q: What is special about the memory of an agent you built?
options: It has its own memory compartment and can't see other agents' memories
It shares one common memory with all the other agents
Memory is fully turned off for agents you build yourself
questions.explain: Every agent gets its own memory cell, isolated from the rest.
